rationale:
Long-form: the playbook's top priority is shipping the Foundayo (orforglipron) what-to-expect video with the 11-20 and 11-21 fact-check fixes. It is an approved drug with a name people search for. The Foundayo Short got 826 views on day 1, and news coverage in Australia, Canada and the UK is rising. It is a re-render of a script that was held and never published, so it doesn't repeat a live video. It is built only from the label, which makes it verifiable in depth. Search-demand formats already make up more than 2 of the last 7 long videos (Mounjaro vs Zepbound, Zepbound vs Wegovy, Months 2–6), so this choice is about the approved-drug priority, not the quota.

Shorts: all three are felt symptoms or practical moments, with the drug named first.
- S1 is the spin-off of L1. It is a myth-flip on a practical moment ("does the Foundayo pill need an empty stomach at Thanksgiving dinner?"), and it links to the Foundayo long video.
- S2 is an early, low-competition "Is this normal?" felt symptom: skin tingling or soreness. The radar marked it caution, so it uses only label figures, says the evidence is limited, names only the drug the evidence covers, and has clear call-your-prescriber lines.
- S3 fills the 20:00 holiday-table slot with a moment we haven't covered yet: family commenting on how little you eat. It is mindset only, with no diet rules, and it links to Thanksgiving.

Nothing repeats an angle from the last 30 days. Injection site, hair, pen storage, pen damage, leftovers, drinks, heartburn, fullness and eating order were all covered recently, so they were skipped. Body systems vary across the day (digestion, skin and nerves, mindset), and no pillar is used more than twice.

pieces.topic: Starting orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect, from the US prescribing information (rev 7/2026) and Medication Guide only. Fixed resubmission of the verified script held on 11-11 and given a REVISE on 11-20 and 11-21 (playbook queue #4). It is not a duplicate of a live video; check the live list first.
pieces.angle: Locked label-only script with every fix applied. s28: 10.3% stopped because of adverse events vs 2.7% on placebo (not 2.6%). s42: the Medication Guide's pancreatitis wording exactly ('with or without vomiting', no 'nausea'). s54: drop 'is requiring' and keep the FDA's 'potential' increased risk for NAION, crediting the 9 Nov 2026 FDA Drug Safety Communication unless the live PI prints it. Keep the 11-20 fixes: 'didn't stop because of adverse events', 'adverse events' never 'side effects', 'weight-related', and 'the label's Trial 1, in adults without diabetes', with the label's top dose giving -11.1% (any 36 mg / -11.2% figure is labelled as trial-only). Add the drug, timeframe and measure on the s31 and s32 cards, and 'your own history of MTC or MEN 2'. Opening: sentence 1 names orforglipron and the question. Never open with a 'Short answer.' label. Sentence 2 is one concrete thing the viewer may feel (food may sit longer, mild queasiness mostly during dose escalation that decreased over time), then the number. Render fixes: masking 0.02 or lower, a full description ending '…whether it's right for you.', and consistent character design between shots. Include the Health Canada and TGA line only if the regulators' own pages confirm both dates. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Publisher: put a ▶ Watch next link to How It Works after the first paragraph.
pieces.why: Playbook priority #1: an approved, searched drug name ('foundayo' already brings us 476 lifetime minutes), Foundayo Shorts are spiking (826 views on day 1), and Australia, Canada and the UK launched it this week. The body rests on settled label evidence.

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) at Thanksgiving dinner: does the GLP-1 pill have to be taken on an empty stomach? What the US label says about food and water
pieces.angle: Orforglipron (Foundayo) at Thanksgiving: does the pill need an empty stomach? By 6 s, give the PI section 2 wording: take it once daily, with or without food, at any time of day (US PI rev 7/2026). Then, as a separate label sentence: nausea is common, mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time. Add 2 untagged tips at most: a smaller first plate and eating slowly. Add the low-blood-sugar caveat for diabetes plus insulin or a sulfonylurea. Then the emergency card in Medication Guide wording, the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't quote 'without food or water restrictions' as label text.
pieces.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill at Thanksgiving: Empty Stomach? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It pairs an approved drug name people search for with a holiday practical moment, which is the pattern behind our 826-view Foundayo Short. | fact-check: This is a good practical myth-flip, and the fact behind it holds up: the US PI says Foundayo is taken once daily, with or without food, at any time of day, and it found no clinically relevant food effect. However, 'without food or water restrictions' is Lilly's marketing and medical-information phrasing. Don't put that phrase in quotes or credit it to the PI unless you find it in the PI text itself. Section 2 of the PI is the source to quote. Don't compare it with other pills (e.g. Rybelsus). Only include a nausea rate vs placebo if it matches L1's verified script exactly. Keep 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time' as its own sentence. The low-blood-sugar caveat covers diabetes plus insulin or a sulfonylurea. Don't imply zero risk otherwise. Use the full emergency card wording and add the scoped don't-stop line. Leave out dose timing schedules and any suggestion to skip or move a dose for the holiday meal.

pieces.topic: Skin feels sore, tingly or sensitive to touch on a GLP-1 medicine (dysesthesia): what's reported, how uncommon it is, and when to tell your prescriber
pieces.angle: Semaglutide (Wegovy): skin sore, tingly or sensitive to touch? It's a known, labeled effect, and it's more common at the higher dose. Give the label's per-arm rates for dysesthesia and related skin-sensation events: 7.2 mg vs 2.4 mg vs placebo, in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, quoted exactly from the live Wegovy PI. Say the cause isn't known. Untagged line: tell your prescriber, especially if it spreads or gets worse. Then the full Medication Guide allergy emergency card with 'right away', the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't mention tirzepatide, and don't use 'uncommon'. New working title: 'Semaglutide (Wegovy): Skin Sore or Tingly to Touch? #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Skin Sore or Tingly to Touch? #shorts
pieces.why: A felt symptom with almost no creator coverage, in the calm 'Is this normal?' format that wins for us. It is early on a rising signal and comes with an evidence-first caution angle. | fact-check: The evidence is about semaglutide, not tirzepatide. Dysesthesia and related altered skin sensations are characterized for semaglutide in the STEP UP trials and the Wegovy labeling. For 7.2 mg (Wegovy HD, FDA-approved 19 Mar 2026), reported rates are about 22–23% vs about 6% on 2.4 mg and 0% on placebo, and STEP UP T2D gave 18.9% / 4.9% / 0%. Tirzepatide has only case reports and FAERS signals, and it isn't listed on the Zepbound or Mounjaro label. The working title 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro)' would therefore misattribute the data, so it has to change. The proposed relief line 'It's reported, and uncommon' is FALSE at 7.2 mg, where it's roughly 1 in 5. 'Uncommon' can't be used. Base the figures on the live Wegovy PI table, not news or Noom or Ro blogs, and give the population (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition) and the comparator. Name the grouped terms only as the label lists them. Say the cause isn't known. Mention the Medsafe NZ March 2026 article as context only if it's needed. Leave out case reports, creams and supplements.

pieces.topic: Family comments at the Thanksgiving table about how little you're eating on tirzepatide: what the label says about appetite, and calm, guilt-free ways to handle the moment
pieces.angle: On tirzepatide and someone says, 'That's all you're eating?' Relief fact, quoted from the Zepbound PI section 12.2: tirzepatide reduces food intake. Untagged tips, 2 at most: a friendly reply ready ahead of time (you don't owe anyone health details), and boxing a plate for later is fine. Mindset: weight is one health measure among many, and the people count as much as the plate. Add the disordered-eating line pointing to the care team, and the diabetes plus insulin or sulfonylurea low-blood-sugar line. Then the on-screen pancreatitis card in Medication Guide wording, the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. No calorie, 'bad food' or eat-less-as-a-goal messaging.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide at Thanksgiving: 'That's All You're Eating?' #shorts
pieces.why: Thanksgiving is in 4 days and holiday-table Shorts are spiking ('still full the morning after' got 504 views on day 1). This is the one table moment we haven't covered yet. | fact-check: This is a supportive, non-shaming social moment, and it fits Life on GLP-1. Fixes: (1) The 'label wording' has to be the Zepbound or Mounjaro PI's actual sentence from section 12.2 (e.g. that tirzepatide lowers body weight and reduces food intake, with GLP-1 described as a regulator of appetite). Open the PI and quote it exactly, or paraphrase it without claiming it's the label's words. (2) The disordered-eating line should point to support without any eating instruction: 'If you've had disordered eating, follow your care team's plan.' That's fine. Don't add anything suggesting eating less is the goal. (3) Add the eating-less safety sign on screen. Use the full Medication Guide pancreatitis wording, 'severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting … right away', and the scoped don't-stop line. (4) Keep the low-blood-sugar line scoped to diabetes plus insulin or a sulfonylurea, without implying zero risk otherwise. (5) Confirm the Thanksgiving long video is actually live before using it as the related-video target. If it isn't, use Side Effects.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) for obstructive sleep apnea: what the US-approved use covers, what AHI (the apnea-hypopnea index) measures, what the two SURMOUNT-OSA randomized trials showed at 52 weeks (one in people not using PAP, one in people using PAP), why weight is linked to sleep apnea, and questions to ask your doctor or sleep clinician
pieces.angle: Same evergreen label-and-trial explainer, with these changes: (a) Thumbnail: 'SLEEP APNEA + TIRZEPATIDE' with subtext 'Fewer breathing pauses? Zepbound trials' (or 'FEWER BREATHING PAUSES?' with 'tirzepatide (Zepbound)' as subtext). One calm, fully drawn, labelled character in bed with a pen, no body imagery, and no snoring promise. (b) Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) for Sleep Apnea: What the Trials Showed'. (c) GI line, exactly as the label puts it: 'Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are common. In the trials, the majority of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea events happened during dose escalation and decreased over time.' Don't use 'mostly'. (d) Give AHI results as events per hour per arm, with group sizes, the population and the measure, for each trial separately. Secondary outcomes only as printed in the paper, with both arms. (e) Keep everything else in the brief: the CPAP don't-stop line, the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, the emergency card for severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting ('right away'), the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice', and the full 'Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you' line, all spoken and shown on screen.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Sleep Apnea: What Trials Show
pieces.why: A broad, approved-use question people search for, backed by settled primary sources (the US label and SURMOUNT-OSA in NEJM). It fills the beyond-weight gap and replaces the dropped Foundayo video without repeating today's Shorts. | fact-check: The topic is sound and in scope. In December 2024 the FDA approved tirzepatide (Zepbound) for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity, and SURMOUNT-OSA (Malhotra et al., NEJM 2024; two 52-week randomized trials, one without PAP and one with PAP) is a strong primary source. There is real search demand for this and it stays useful for months. It fits the 'Benefits beyond weight' pillar. The safety rules in the brief (CPAP don't-stop line, low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, tirzepatide pancreatitis wording, no dosing or switching) are correct. Three things need fixing before scripting. (1) The thumbnail 'SNORING LESS?' promises something the video can't back up. The trials' main measure was AHI (breathing pauses or shallow breaths per hour), and snoring wasn't a reported endpoint, so the title and thumbnail would oversell. (2) The GI line in the brief, 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time', isn't the label's wording. The Zepbound PI says 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time', and our craft rules ban adding 'mostly'. Copy the label sentence. (3) Chapter 4 secondary results must come only from the NEJM paper or PubMed record, with both arms (for example the sleep-impairment and sleep-disturbance scores, oxygen-drop measures, blood pressure), and no causal 'because of weight loss' wording unless the paper says it. Keep every AHI figure in events per hour, with each trial's population (adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and obesity, without diabetes; no PAP vs using PAP) and the right measure ('counting everyone who started' vs 'if everyone stayed on treatment'). Don't compare the two trials as if they were head-to-head. Quote Section 1 from the 28 Aug 2026 PI word for word. Open with a sentence 1 that asks the question, without a 'Short answer.' label.
